claims.text: The starting material is the HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high-entropy alloy.
The alloy has a quasi-static yield strength of approximately 786 MPa.
The alloy has a quasi-static compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
The alloy has a quasi-static fracture strain of approximately 13.5%.
Solution treatment followed by aging at 800–950 °C for 1–3 hours will induce uniformly distributed nanoscale ordered precipitates in HfZrTiTa0.53.
The aging treatment may produce an ordered second phase such as B2 nanoprecipitates.
The nanoscale precipitates will be embedded in a BCC matrix.
The nanoprecipitates will impede dislocation motion.
Precipitate-induced resistance to dislocation motion will enhance forest hardening.
Enhanced hardening will delay the initiation of adiabatic shear bands.
The aged alloy will exhibit improved uniform plastic deformation under dynamic loading.
The aged alloy will resist rapid failure and shear localization better than the untreated alloy.
The aged alloy will have a dynamic yield strength greater than 850 MPa.
The aged alloy will have a dynamic compressive strength greater than 1500 MPa.
The aged alloy may achieve a dynamic fracture strain greater than 15%.
Delayed localization will produce a more controlled and progressive release of impact-induced energy.
The prediction is scoped to adiabatic dynamic compression at strain rates from 1000 to 3000 s⁻¹.
Over-aging may cause precipitate coarsening and embrittlement, reducing the proposed benefit.

contradictions.description: The numerical predictions are described as changes relative to quasi-static baseline values, whereas the matched experiment compares aged and untreated specimens under dynamic loading. Quasi-static and dynamic strengths and fracture strains are not directly equivalent comparators, so the reference used to evaluate the numerical predictions is internally inconsistent.
